opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that trust, for most of human history, has been built on explanation. When a doctor tells you that you need surgery, you may not understand the medicine yourself, but you know there's a chain of reasoning behind it: a textbook, a training process, peers who could check the work. Even if you never verify it, the possibility of verification is what makes you comfortable. With large AI models, that chain is broken in a strange way. The system can give you an answer, and often a very good one, but even the people who built it can't fully trace why it arrived there. So we're being asked to accept results on the basis of track record alone, and that's psychologically and institutionally very different.

There are a few layers to this. The first is accountability. If an AI system denies someone a loan, flags a medical scan, or recommends a legal strategy, and it turns out to be wrong, who is responsible? Our legal and professional systems assume that a decision can be reconstructed and someone can be asked, "Why did you do this?" When the honest answer is "the model's internal weights produced this output," that doesn't fit any framework we have.

The second is the problem of errors that look like successes. These systems are very fluent. They can produce an answer that is confident, well-structured, and completely wrong, and because we can't inspect the reasoning, we often can't tell the difference until something goes wrong downstream. With a human expert, hesitation or inconsistency gives you signals. With a model, the surface quality is almost always high, so the usual cues we rely on don't work.

The third is generalization. A model may perform extremely well on the cases we've tested, but without understanding its internal mechanisms, we don't really know where its boundaries are. It might be relying on some shortcut or spurious correlation that holds in the test data and fails badly in the real world. In high-stakes areas like healthcare, autonomous driving, or scientific discovery, that uncertainty about the edges is exactly what makes people nervous.

And finally there's a cultural dimension. Scientists in particular are trained to value understanding over prediction. If an AI system predicts a protein structure or proposes a new material, it's genuinely useful, but many researchers feel uneasy calling it knowledge if no one can explain why it works. We may be entering a period where we have to separate those two things, accepting that some tools are reliable without being interpretable, much like we used many medicines for decades before understanding their mechanisms.

So I don't think the answer is to reject these systems, but rather to build new forms of trust: rigorous testing, interpretability research that opens up the black box bit by bit, and clear human responsibility at the points where decisions actually matter. Trust has to be earned in a different way now, and I think we're only at the very beginning of figuring out what that looks like.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first difficulty is actually a cultural one, not a technical one. In science we were trained for a long time to believe that a result only counts if you can trace the chain of reasoning behind it. When I did my PhD work, if I showed my advisor a measurement, the first question was always "why does this happen," not "does it work." So when an AI system hands you an answer and the honest truth is that nobody, including the people who built it, can fully explain the path to that answer, it collides with a very deep instinct about what knowledge is supposed to look like.

The second difficulty is more practical. If you don't understand how a system arrives at a result, you also don't understand where it will fail. A model can be right ninety-five percent of the time, and that sounds great, until you realize you have no principled way to know which five percent you're in. In my own field, materials and condensed matter physics, that matters a lot. If a model predicts a new material will be a superconductor, I can go synthesize it and check. The experiment is the ground truth, so the opacity of the model is tolerable, because nature gives me the final verdict. But in domains where you can't cheaply run the experiment, medicine, policy, law, that verification loop is missing, and then trusting the output becomes a much harder decision.

I'd also say there is a third issue, which is what happens to the humans in the loop. If people get used to accepting answers they can't interrogate, the skill of interrogation atrophies. Scientists are supposed to be professional skeptics. I worry less about whether the AI is right and more about whether we stop asking.

That said, I don't think the answer is to refuse these results. Physicists have accepted things we couldn't fully explain before. High-temperature superconductivity has been used in real devices for decades, and we still argue about the mechanism. What made it acceptable was reproducibility and independent verification, not a complete theory. So my view is that we should stop demanding full interpretability as the price of admission, and instead build the same kind of infrastructure we have for experiments: reproducibility, error bars, adversarial testing, and a clear understanding of where the system has been validated and where it hasn't. Treat the AI less like an oracle and more like a new instrument whose calibration you have to earn.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difficulty is knowing when to trust the result. If an AI gives you an answer that you can independently verify, then not understanding its internal workings may be acceptable. But if you’re asking it a question precisely because you don’t know the answer, how do you judge whether it’s right?

A convincing explanation doesn’t necessarily solve that problem, either. The explanation itself could be wrong. We need ways to test the result, understand where the system tends to fail, and recognize when it’s operating beyond what we’ve tested.

And the stakes matter. If it recommends a movie, we can tolerate mistakes. If it informs a medical decision, we need much stronger evidence and clear responsibility. So accepting these systems isn’t simply a question of whether we understand every step. It’s whether we have enough evidence to justify trusting them in a particular situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that accepting a result and trusting the process that produced it are two different things. An AI system can give you an answer that looks right, but if you don’t understand why it arrived at that answer, it’s hard to know when you should rely on it and when you should be skeptical.

That matters especially when something goes wrong. Was the problem in the data, the model, or the way we asked the question? And who takes responsibility for the decision? If we can’t investigate those questions, it becomes difficult to build trust.

Of course, we don’t fully understand every system we already rely on. So I don’t think complete understanding has to be a prerequisite. But we need ways to test the results independently, understand the limits, and make the level of scrutiny proportional to the consequences. Accepting an AI recommendation for a movie is very different from accepting one for medical treatment.
